intent: A Grand View Estates homeowner wants an artificial lawn, dog area or putting green and needs to know what is different about this lot: water comes from a private exempt well rather than a utility, the house is on septic, the ground ranges from steep gravelly slopes to clay loam and a flood-rated alluvial strip, and the neighborhood association is voluntary with no zoning authority.
distinctValue: Every neighbouring page (Stonegate, Meridian, Lone Tree) describes utility water with assigned watering days, and Foxfield's well rules come from its own town code in Arapahoe County. Grand View Estates has none of that. The page leads with the rule that actually governs outdoor water here, the well permit: DWR Guideline 2023-1 says exempt permits issued under the presumption statute on parcels under 35 acres are limited to household use inside one single-family dwelling with no outdoor uses, while other permits (including registrations of wells used before May 8, 1972, and Denver Basin permits under 37-92-602(3)(b)(I)) can allow up to one acre of home gardens and lawns; the association says most lots are two acres and the first well permit here dates to 1956, so the page does not guess which applies and sends the reader to DWR's Well Permit Search, whose file lists allowable uses. It flags that a household-use-only permit counts washing outdoor features as outside use (relevant to rinsing pet turf) and that trading lawn irrigation for another use requires re-permitting. It explains the Denver Basin groundwater is non-renewable (DWR) and what GERWCD is (ballot-formed local government, 1.5 mill levy, USGS monitoring). It applies Colorado Regulation 43 to turf planning: no compaction of the soil treatment area from vehicles, livestock, recreational use or site development, and a final cover of soil suitable for vegetation at least ten inches deep graded to divert stormwater, so the base stays off the field. It reports USDA SSURGO map units measured inside the Census CDP boundary (Newlin gravelly sandy loam 8 to 30 percent slopes the largest share, Fondis clay loam up to 45 percent clay, Satanta loam, loamy alluvial land rated for frequent flooding). It routes zoning questions to Douglas County, because the association's FAQ says its board has no authority over zoning violations. Unsettled points become questions to named offices: DWR (outdoor rinsing on a household-use-only permit), Douglas County Health Department (permit record showing where the septic system sits), Douglas County (mapped floodplain; zoning). Douglas County's own well, septic and zoning pages (douglasco.gov) returned a Cloudflare challenge on 2026-09-12 and were not read, so nothing on the page relies on them; FEMA's NFHL service timed out, so the page states no flood zone.

sources.label: Grandview Estates Rural Water Conservation District: About
supports: Grandview Estates Rural Water Conservation District (GERWCD) is a Colorado State recognized agency that exists to protect the water interests of Grandview Estates residents.
Grandview Estates is one of Douglas County’s first neighborhoods and is located on the Northside of Lincoln Ave. adjacent to S. Chambers Rd bordering the Western edge of Parker, Colorado.
GERWCD was formed after a ballot vote in November of 2007 to serve as a local government agency to facilitate water resource management, development, and conservation in Grandview Estates
Programs include researching and monitoring water supply, protecting individual exempt well supply, and quality from outside influences.
Each property owner pays a small 1.5 mill levy tax annually to the District based on their assessed property value.

Historically, these funds have been utilized to fund the USGS well level and quality monitoring programs, water quality testing, adjudication of water rights, defense of water rights, annual financial reviews, and keeping residents aware of a variety of potential water issues surrounding Grandview Estates due to the recent development within Douglas County (including Chambers Reservoir).
Page rendered as 720-987-9701.

sources.label: Colorado Division of Water Resources: Guideline 2023-1, Uses of Water From Exempt and Small Capacity Wells (24-page PDF)
supports: Guideline 2023-1 Uses of Water From Exempt and Small Capacity Wells

Section 37-92-602 of the Colorado Revised Statutes (C.R.S.) provides an exemption from administration in the water right priority system for wells located outside of Designated Groundwater Basins with uses limited to those in section 37-92-602(1). Those uses are specifically identified as ordinary household purposes, fire protection and fire-fighting, the watering of poultry, domestic animals, and livestock on farms and ranches, the irrigation of not over one acre of home gardens and lawns, monitoring and observation purposes, and drinking and sanitary facilities in individual commercial businesses.

Exempt well permits issued pursuant to section 37-92-602(3)(b)(II)(A) on parcels less than 35 acres, which are not on parcels created through a cluster development, are limited to ordinary household purposes inside one single-family dwelling, with no allowed outdoor uses.

Pursuant to section 37-92-602(3)(b)(I) which requires that the State Engineer find that the well will not result in injury to the vested water rights of others or any other existing well. Such wells are generally issued to withdraw water from nontributary aquifers; certain Denver Basin aquifers
Pursuant to section 37-92-602(5) for the registration of existing wells that were put to beneficial use prior to May 8, 1972 for uses allowed under section 37-92-602(1).
Uses of water from the Denver Basin and nontributary sources may be limited to the quantity of available groundwater underlying the lot for both exempt and small capacity wells.

Use of water outside of the dwelling structure including, but not limited to: Growing plants that are not inside the dwelling, including those grown in a greenhouse; Washing vehicles, windows, decks, or other outdoor features.

11.1 Trading allowed uses for wells in Denver Basin aquifers ... the allowed uses may be traded as long as the amount of water required to serve the modified uses does not exceed the amount of water required for the existing uses
The irrigation of 1,000 square-feet of home lawn and garden - 0.05 acre-feet per year.
In order to modify the uses allowed by the well permit, the holder of the well permit must apply to re-permit the well by submitting a well permit application and filing fee.

For instance, a water user may not obtain an exempt well permit that trades the irrigation of one acre of home gardens and lawns for the filling of a swimming pool, even if the swimming pool water use is measured to be less than the irrigation use.

sources.label: Colorado Division of Water Resources: Denver Basin
supports: The aquifers in the Denver Basin are called, progressing from top to bottom, the Dawson, Denver, Arapahoe, and Laramie-Fox Hills aquifers.

Because of the nature of the confining layers and because of the limited connection between these aquifers and surface water, the groundwater in the aquifers is not renewable. When the groundwater is used, it is being “mined” or used up without any replacement.

a landowner ... is limited to withdrawing only that quantity of water determined to be available underlying the land. Additionally, Senate Bill 213 limited withdrawals on the basis of an aquifer life of one hundred years, which is administered by limiting average annual withdrawals to one percent of the volume of water that is determined to be available underlying the land.

The premises of the quantity of groundwater available based on the amount underlying the land and limiting annual withdrawals to one percent of the total amount are also used to allow the uses permitted for many exempt well permits issued for individual on-lot wells that use Denver Basin groundwater.

sources.label: Colorado Water Quality Control Commission: Regulation No. 43, On-Site Wastewater Treatment System Regulation (5 CCR 1002-43), consolidated text
supports: REGULATION NO. 43 - ON-SITE WASTEWATER TREATMENT SYSTEM REGULATION 5 CCR 1002-43
ADOPTED: April 1, 2026 EFFECTIVE: May 19, 2026

43.8 J. Surface Activity: Activity or use on the surface of the ground over any part of the OWTS must be restricted. The soil treatment area must not be subject to damage or soil compaction from livestock, vehicular traffic, recreational use, or other site development activity. Construction equipment not necessary to install the OWTS must be kept off of the soil treatment area to prevent undesirable compaction of the soils.

43.10 f. A final cover of soil suitable for vegetation at least ten inches deep must be placed from the top of the geotextile or similar pervious material in a rock and pipe system, chamber, or manufactured media, up to the final surface grade of the soil treatment area.
43.10 g. Following construction, the ground surface must be graded to divert stormwater runoff or other outside water from the soil treatment area. The area must be protected against erosion.

43.10 h. Backfilling and compaction of soil treatment areas must be accomplished in a manner that does not impair the intended function and performance of the storage/distribution media and soil and distribution laterals, allows for the establishment of vegetative cover, minimizes settlement and maintains proper drainage.
